subtopic: MEDICAL AND HOSPITAL COVERAGE FOR IMMIGRANTS
MEDICAL AND HOSPITAL COVERAGE FOR IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:
1.	Have the Departments of National Health and Welfare and/or Manpower and Immigration received any representations from International Services of London requesting coverage for new immigrants to Canada of basic hospital protection for their first three months in this country in order to assist these new-comers?
2.	Have either or both of these departments received from the same source representations to allow monetary or other consideration for newly arriving pregnant wives and, if so, what consideration has been given?

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Bechard (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: MEDICAL AND HOSPITAL COVERAGE FOR IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:
The Ministers of National Health and Welfare and Manpower and Immigration inform me that representations were made by International House of London concerning medical and hospitalization expenses incurred by newly arrived immigrants. Various arrangements have been in effect for many years to ensure adequate protection against such expenses during an immigrant's initial period of establishment in Canada, but only where the newcomer is not in a position to pay these costs himself.
Essentially, this coverage extends only to immigrants who become indigent or who are in receipt of some form of assistance from the Department of Manpower and Immigration. The representations in question go much further than this and suggest some form of protection for newcomers who might have their successful establishment jeopardized through the dissipation of all of their available capital by unexpected medical expenses. A study is being made to see what further measures might be considered.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of National Revenue and ask whether he is now prepared to table the letter which the officials of his department gave to Volkswagen approving the sale of some 10,000 cars to Studebaker, which cars were imported into Canada and later resold to Canadian Volkswagen, resulting in a loss to the treasury of some $2 million. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure that all hon. members appreciate the role which the National Housing Act has played in the Canadian economy and appreciate the fact that this role has been most impressive during recent years. Perhaps I might add that I am certain that as we progress in a more advanced and complex society that act will have an increasingly significant impact on our human environment in Canada. If it is to do this, further amendments to the National Housing Act are, of course, to be expected from time to time.
Before offering a detailed explanation of the resolution now before the committee it might be appropriate-in fact, in my opinion it would be decidedly helpful-for me to make a statement concerning Canada's housing experience so far during the year 1966 and the impact which our housing statute has brought to bear on the economic and social fabric of our country. May I say at the outset that, although the role of the National Housing Act has been impressive, I realize all too well that this is not going to be one of the most successful years in the housing field, for a number of reasons. Perhaps the primary reason is that the forces which have dominated the entire economy during this past year continue to exert a major influence on the housing scene. Hon. members perhaps will recall that several months ago in this chamber I sounded a warning that after four successive years of rising housing output, reaching a record of 166,000 units last year, we must expect a marked drop in the rate of our residential growth in the year 1966. Figures now available for the first nine months of this year show that performance is more or less in accord with the levels of activity which we anticipated when I made that statement.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Between January 1 and the end of September of this year, 75,727 new dwellings were started in Canada in urban centres, as well as a much smaller number in the rural areas. This is a decrease in the urban centres of 23 per cent from the record achievement of some 98,000-odd in the same period in 1965. For the most part the decline was registered in the area of multiple dwelling construction, where there is a decrease of 34 per cent compared with a drop of only 6.3 per cent in the volume of single dwellings. Behind this slackened production rate, of course, is the fact that Canada today is developing at a pace exceeding any growth period in our

October 26, 1966
National Housing Act
history, a pace which I said during the course of the budget debate, and others have said also, in my view is too rapid for our own economic well-being.
The multitude of new projects that are being pressed forward in all areas of our national expansion have placed at a premium every dollar of investment funds available. One has to think only of my adopted province of British Columbia where we have under construction multimillions of dollars worth of plant in the forest industry alone. All these things require investment in office buildings and service buildings in different parts of the province, and that is in one industry only. The fact remains that, as I have said, every dollar is at a premium from the standpoint of investment. Perhaps that is not surprising because in a free enterprise economy money generally goes where the rewards are the greatest, and it is difficult for anyone who favours a free enterprise economy and a political philosophy based on free enterprise to be too critical of the efforts of our investors to channel their funds into areas where they will get the best interest rates, so long as these rates are not usurious or are not unreasonable.
The signs and portents of the current situation were obvious some time ago. All hon. members will recall perhaps that it was with that background, and on my advice as the minister responsible for the administration of the National Housing Act, that in January of this year the government raised the interest rate on mortgages from 6J per cent to 6| per cent. As a result of that action there was a noticeable resurgence of activity for a short time. That was particularly true during the months of January and February, but as more attractive opportunities for investment emerged out of the continuing intense competition for long term funds the advantage of this 2 per cent increase in the interest rate dimmed. Traditional lenders in respect of multiple dwelling investment withdrew their participation. This development, of course, did not come as a complete surprise, because as I have said more than once, the interest rate itself cannot work miracles; it can help, but when the competition becomes acute it falls short of the objectives that are set.
Nevertheless I can assure you that the rate, which now is at 6f per cent, is under continuous study. The fact that in respect of the bill now pending before a committee of this house a recommendation has been made

to parliament that the bank interest rate should be raised possibly to 7 per cent will necessitate further immediate study in this direction, and I may say that that study now is underway. The result of the competition, which we have had to date for funds, is that there have been practically no funds available for certain types of new residential construction this year since the beginning of March, except those funds made available by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation under the National Housing Act.
Despite the great need for an increased level of insured loans during 1966, I think it can safely be said that the National Housing Act actually is making a greater contribution to housing starts this year than in the record year 1965. I am sure members of the house will be interested to know that up to September 30 this year the number of applications for direct loans totalled approximately 45,000, an increase over last year's figure at this same date. Of this year's total number of dwellings, more than 32,000 were proposed for construction with direct loans from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. That figure of 32,000 is almost 10,000 above the number recorded for the whole of 1965.
There is little doubt-and I referred to this in an answer I gave in this chamber within the last few days-that the volume of direct lending by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in Canada will accelerate even further as this year's winter housebuilding program gains momentum. It is noteworthy that notwithstanding the cancellation of the $500 bonus payment offered in the programs of the three preceding winters, applications for houses to be constructed during the coming winter, 1966-67, are running well ahead of last year when there was the special $500 winter bonus. With the extended period of eligibility for assistance this year, I am convinced that we can look forward to a program this winter at least equal to if not better than that of last year.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
This program is especially significant under the circumstances that now prevail because without these direct loans thousands of families in Canada would not be able to get the new dwellings which they would like. I think I should make it clear that the government intends to pursue the course it has been following, but it is not our intention to pick up all of the slack that has resulted from the substantial withdrawal by private lenders from the residential field.
October 26, 1966

The work that we are doing in respect of these 32,000-odd houses represents an investment by the federal government of upward of $500 million or perhaps closer to $600 million or even $700 million. In this atmosphere of unparalleled economic expansion I think it would be unwise, and I am perfectly sure that most members of the house, if not all, will agree, if we were to channel in addition to the $600 million or so that I have mentioned further vast sums of public funds into the housebuilding field at this time. I am sure members will agree that such a course would be contrary to the government's policy of levelling out or extending our period of prosperity.
It has been and is our intention to ensure that funds allocated primarily for housing are utilized in those areas which hold the greatest potential for Canada's social and economic improvement as a whole. Let me refer here to the efforts that are being made in all parts of Canada to improve the living conditions of elderly people and to provide decent and healthful accommodations for families whose incomes deny them the ability to maintain homes on the open market. It is also our intention to help house the increasing number of university students who are seeking to live near universities while they are carrying on their studies.
At the same time there has been no hesitation and no hold-back in respect of federal government aid to the growing number of municipalities which are embarking on programs of civic improvement with National Housing Act assistance, and to certain other municipalities with special needs. This is most important to resource based communities in this country. We do not intend to relax for one moment our support in the provision of housing to serve the needs of the scores of vital new communities which are mushrooming into existence in the remote areas of all of our provinces and coming into existence to develop our natural resources.
In this connection I will never forget my impression of the tremendous development that is currently taking place in northern Alberta, in connection with the oil sands at Fort McMurray. Some 10 or 12 days ago I visited this richest known deposit of oil in the world. Hundreds of millions of dollars are being poured into this development, and houses must be provided. The same applies to the potash towns in Saskatchewan and to communities such as Gold River, Mackenzie,
National Housing Act
Prince George and others in British Columbia, as well as to new towns in Ontario, Quebec and Newfoundland where our minerals and forestry resources are being developed at an impressive rate.
I am sure that anyone who is interested in social and economic benefits in this country will agree that none of these programs to which I have referred could possibly be curtailed. Despite the difficulties that we are having in financing housing we have managed to keep these housing ventures going at an encouraging level.
It might be well if I also referred to the record attained in the area of university housing projects. Twenty five loans have been made during the current year, totalling approximately $37 million, in most of the ten provinces for the provision of modern living quarters for approximately 6,000 students. This nine month total in housing loans for students is far in excess of the activity for the full year 1965 when less than $12 million was authorized. Incidentally, just within the last four or five days we have announced a loan to the Ontario Student Housing Corporation of nearly $12 million, $11,634,000, to be exact, to build the first part of the largest university housing complex in Canada. It is to be built on the campus of the University of Guelph and it will house nearly 1,700 students.
Equal success has been attained in our efforts across Canada to meet some of the serious and pressing needs for housing for low income families and especially for elderly persons. To the end of September, 42 such loans with an aggregate value of approximately $13 million had been approved for projects sponsored by non-profit organizations. This will provide roughly 1,100 self-contained housing units and hospital accommodation for more than 1,000 more people. This compares very favourably with the $14.2 million in 1965 for the development of approximately the same number of units.
Seven federal-provincial housing projects, providing 553 low-rental dwellings, have also been authorized as against four in 1965. There are a number of other achievements that I would like to refer to regarding what we have done in housing in the northern parts of the prairie provinces for the Indians and Metis who have left the reserves, and what we are doing in the Northwest Territories in the field of housing, but time does not permit. What I have referred to represents just some of the achievements that are

October 26, 1966
National Housing Act
being made today to meet these serious and urgent social needs. If these improved activities are to continue and if even greater progress is to be made in the over-all improvement of living conditions in Canada, we must be prepared to take new and additional steps through the refashioning of the National Housing Act.
During the past two years I have met and discussed with the provincial ministers who are my opposite numbers in all ten of the provinces, how the amendments to the National Housing Act which were made in 1964 and in 1965 have been working out. As a result of our discussions and out of the different symposia that have been held, some 10 or 11 across Canada, have come a number of good suggestions. Not all of them can be incorporated in the bill which I hope to introduce in the house shortly, because in the economic climate that now prevails that would be an unwise thing to do, at least in the opinion of the government. There are, however, a number of improvements that are urgent and imperative, and it is for this reason I have no hesitation in putting them forward at this time.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
To begin with, the government proposes in the resolution now being considered that the National Housing Act be amended so as to provide for the first time that loans may be made to persons who wish to purchase, improve and occupy existing housing. It is proposed that these loans will carry conditions similar to those which are now made in respect of new housing. While it is true that restricting National Housing Act lending to new houses largely accounts for the rapid expansion in housing starts and improved housing conditions during the last five or six years, there are in this country many potential home owners who simply cannot afford the luxury of new housing. To buy a house that people in the income tax bracket of over $10,000 a year would like to occupy represents an investment, I am told, of between $17,000 and $25,000 and, depending upon one's financial ability to finance, it might cost considerably more than that.
In communities like Windsor, a city with which I am somewhat familiar, many people are leaving the rural areas and moving into the city, and they require housing. This situation exists in other cities in this country. The only hope these people have of obtaining a house of their own rather than living in rented quarters is to buy an existing house

and repair it. There are many houses in all parts of this country, some built in the last century and others in the first decade or two of this century which, if modern heating, electrical and plumbing systems were installed, would provide very good homes with another 40 or 50 years of economic use.

We believe that we may be able to improve the investment by traditional lenders and merchant builders by increasing the loan ratio. If any one of the housing corporations of the provinces wishes to borrow money today for housing, it can obtain up to 90 per cent of the value of the building; for instance, we will lend the Ontario Housing Corporation or the Quebec Housing Corporation 90 per cent of the value of the building. In the traditional construction industry, it is 85 per cent. We want to remove this discrimination and intend proposing that this level be increased to 90 per cent to make the situation uniform.
I am sure hon. members understand that there is throughout the country a great demand for new houses, and I believe we will improve this situation materially by the two changes to which I have just referred. We are also asking parliament to increase the $200 million that is available under the present act for university housing projects. We want to raise this figure to $350 million. The number of requests for loans in this respect is increasing to such an extent that we certainly will have to raise the level appreciably. The university population has increased very rapidly, as every hon. member knows. Full time university enrolment has risen tremendously. Two of our universities in British Columbia have, I believe, risen in population this year, one by approximately 600 and the other by over 1,000. British Columbia is the province I am most familiar with, but I know that the same situation exists all over Canada.
Until recently only a few universities were able to house out-of-town students on or near campus, but since the National Housing Act was introduced-and here I must give credit

October 26. 1966
National Housing Act
to the former government for introducing this improvement, which has been a very significant one-during the last six years loans for university housing have risen to the extent that housing accommodation is provided on or near campus for over 30,000 Canadian university students. The fact that today we are seeking additional funds to allow C.M.H.C. to carry on this essential program is an indication, based on detailed surveys in conjunction with the provinces, that there are still enormous residential shortages by the universities in every province in Canada.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
But as you will have noticed, this resolution seeks more than just an increase in funds to enable the university housing projects to continue. It also proposes that the National Housing Act be amended for the purpose of making loans, with the concurrence of the provincial governments concerned, for housing projects which will not be restricted to just university housing. The government has in mind, and this again comes out of the 11 symposia that were held across the country, housing projects for such institutions as vocational and training schools, training hospitals for nurses, and schools for special groups of handicapped people. All these groups have housing problems. For instance, Ontario contemplates the building of six community colleges. We know that Ry-erson is handicapped today and is badly in need of additional residential accommodation. It has been pleading for help for the past three years to my knowledge. If this amendment is accepted by parliament it will enable us to make loans for housing to institutions of this nature.

In this legislation we also seek to extend for an additional three years the period within which the construction of a sewage treatment project must be completed if the municipality concerned is to be forgiven payment of a part of the principal amount of the loan and of the accrued interest. The government proposes that the forgiveness date for

loans made on sewage treatment projects be extended from March 31, 1967 to March 31, 1970. Our intention to do so was announced by the Prime Minister a little more than a year ago and was reaffirmed by me in this house earlier this year. I might say that the continued expansion of our urban areas has certainly rendered inadequate sewage system plants constructed even as recently as 20 years ago. I myself know of this from the inspections I have made.
Sewage continues to be poured into the country's streams and rivers, but much has been accomplished. The program to create employment introduced by the former government during the period of recession has not only helped to provide employment but has performed a very worth while service for the people of Canada in helping to clear up the pollution that exists in too many of our streams and lakes.
I think hon. members will be interested to hear the following figures. More than 1,000 loans have been made during the past five or six years to municipalities in every province to combat water and soil pollution; yet much remains to be done. Had we not asked for this extension, which we are now doing formally, many municipalities would have tried to rush to completion before March sewage facilities which they should take longer to plan and to instal and which we certainly hope they will be able to instal economically when the demand for expert workers is at a lower level than it is today. Furthermore, without this incentive of a 25 per cent forgiveness of principal and interest, many projects might never be started and many new projects which we hope will come forward in the months directly ahead might never be started because of a shortage of money.

Under the act we have authority to spend an aggregate $8.5 billion. Mr. Chairman, we have just heard the minister speak on the resolution which, although quite lengthy and comprising some seven separate programs, could be summarized as a request for additional funds for housing in Canada. The only factor that is new in the resolution relates to the right to purchase existing housing. May I remind the committee that this is part of the policy of our party and we are very happy to see it incorporated in the resolution.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
In his opening remarks the minister admitted that this has not been the most successful 23033-578
National Housing Act
year for housing in Canada, that the economic expansion has been too rapid for social and human welfare. We also have to admit that this has not been the most successful year and possibly the reason for this situation is the lack of long term planning of housing in Canada. I believe this matter has been raised many times before, but it seems we use housing as a buffer. We use it in boom periods and we use it in times of recession, but in a reverse way. This reminds me of a one-piston engine. When times are good we push the piston in and when times are bad we pull the piston out. I believe the construction industry is too important to be pushed around in this way by the legislators of our country. As everyone knows, the construction industry is very important. It is about the second largest industry and it ranks fifth in the number of people employed. These two factors alone should prove the importance of the housing industry to our country.
A few minutes ago the minister referred to expansion as being too rapid. I am wondering whether he is implying that the shortage of funds results solely from the boom period through which we are passing? May we not also say it is possibly a result of the failure to introduce the Bank Act amendments? If they had been introduced in 1965 there would have been funds available through the banking institutions for mortgage purposes. I believe the government is at fault for not having introduced the bank legislation early enough to have been of benefit to the housing industry in Canada in 1966.
There is another factor which has possibly contributed to the reduction in the amount of construction in the housing industry. I refer to the 11 per cent sales tax which was imposed by this government on building materials. As you are aware, Mr. Chairman, the majority of Canadians who build homes or who have homes built are not people who have much in the way of savings. They are people who from the time they are born have one hope and that is to some day own their own home. During a period of years they try to save whatever they can, and one day take the plunge to get a home for themselves. When you add the 11 per cent sales tax to the cost of a house you are discouraging many of these people who would be able to own their own homes and who would not have to go to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for the funds required to build their homes. They may be able to contribute some $4,000 or $5,000 toward the cost of a $12,000 or

October 26, 1966
National Housing Act
$14,000 house. The fact is these people are not building homes because of the imposition of the 11 per cent sales tax. This tax itself has contributed to inflation. It is one of the many factors which have delayed housing construction in Canada.
When I speak about the long term policy of the government, I am thinking of the immigration policy which will be coming before us shortly. We expect there will be 125,000 or
150,000	immigrants coming to Canada each year. We are in a period in which the war babies of 1945 and 1946 are now approaching the age of marriage. It is anticipated that by 1970 we are going to need at least a million homes. This is a rather serious position in which to be. We are just concluding the year 1966, and in a four year period we will have to build one million homes in Canada. I believe that the government has delayed looking into this problem. Last year the long term aspect of the problem was emphasized so that by 1970 we would be able to supply these people with the houses they would require.
I have noted that the main weakness of the National Housing Act continues to be its urban nature. Somehow we must help the fellow who lives in the village or in the countryside. I was very happy, however, to hear the minister state some time ago that regional offices were to be opened in some of the rural areas of the country. Here again the problem is that there are not sufficient funds for mortgage purposes and there are not sufficient personnel to advise those who would like to build homes. We are slow in giving the service these people require.
I was happy to learn that if the private lenders do not make the necessary funds available, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will make direct loans. As I have said before, it is very important that this legislation be brought forward. However, it seems to me that today legislation should have been introduced concerning the senior citizens of our country because many of these people are living in homes that need repair. Many of them do not have the necessary means to undertake these repairs. If legislation of this nature had been introduced, we would be satisfying one segment of our economy involving people who are today crying for help from our governments.
These are the points of immediate concern. Pressure has come from all the building associations across Canada and I believe that pressure is justified because these people, as I have said, create jobs. However, the industry has been used as a buffer. There is no reason

for this because there is an urgent need for housing. What are we doing to stabilize the industry? During one period of the year people engaged in the industry are working and during the next six months they are not. Those who are engaged in research and design are rather important to an industry such as this. I should like to impress upon the minister again the need for a long term policy in connection with housebuilding in Canada.
I am very happy to learn that the minister is extending the sewage treatment project scheme under this act. This is one of our recommendations, and it is a provision that is important to the health and welfare of Canadians. We believe it should be made a permanent piece of legislation.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I do not see anything whatever concerning the Municipal Development and Loan Act. As the minister mentioned earlier today, I realize that this matter is administered by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, but it does come under the responsibility of the Minister of Finance. I am very distressed to know that there will be no extension of this act, or so I have been informed.

With regard to housing projects for university students, I have my feelings on this subject but I would say that as far as loans for such projects on campuses of vocational or technical schools are concerned this is a measure to be commended provided, as the minister stated, the approval and consent of the province concerned are obtained. I am not going to prolong further the passage of the resolution; I simply wanted to make those few remarks. Once again I request the government to bring in a long-term

policy on housing at which we could have a good look. This would enable us to know for the next five years exactly where the industry is going to stand and how we are going to look after those who will require houses during that period.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened to the minister today with rather mixed feelings. First of all I had a feeling of great pleasure that finally the government was taking some new steps with regard to the housing situation in this country. However, to offset that the minister unfortunately did what so many ministers in the past have done. He talked about the forces affecting the economy, mouthed meaningless records that have nothing to do with the need for housing in this country, and used such expressions as "Last year showed a greater growth in housing than any growth in history". What in the world does that mean if you do not compare it with the actual need for housing in this country? It is meaningless; it is gobbledygook.
The record over the last ten years or so that 1 have been in this house indicates that every amendment which has been made to the housing act-and there has been at least one at almost every session of parliament since I have been here-has been putting one patch on another patch. There has never been bold leadership in the field, never any cognizance of what is the trouble and then trying to cope with it. When the forces of the economy have pushed the government to take one little step, they have then tried to claim great credit for it. Instead of looking at the problem and facing up to it by embarking upon a program to cope with it, housing has been used merely as a pressure gauge by this government, the government before it and the government before that. What we have had under these governments has been a steady procession of booms and busts. They have used housing as the number one weapon to bust the boom or to boom the bust, whatever the case may have been at any particular time.
However, in the resolution before us today there is for the first time a new factor in the housing field. We are very pleased to see the emergence of this new factor because it is one that we have recommended for many years both to this government and to the one before it. At long last the government is taking some new steps in this field. The government has at least taken a short step
National Housing Act
toward solving some of the housing problems facing us in Canada.
If this measure is carried through with vigour, it can achieve most excellent results. If on the other hand, as has happened far too often in the past, this is just more windowdressing, then it will be seen to amount to nothing else but that. I give one word of warning to the government. The people of Canada are not as easily fooled today as they have been in the past, and if this is just windowdressing the people of Canada will see through it very quickly.
The history of the action taken by the government in regard to housing has been a pretty sorry one in spite of the headlines we have seen from time to time. The government has always tried to make a virtue out of necessity. I noticed that a recent special study conducted by the Organization of Economic Co-operation and Development, O.E.C.D., shows that between the years 1953 to 1963 Canada slipped from fifth place to ninth place among 15 countries in North America and Western Europe with regard to meeting housing needs. Most damning of all is the fact that in this period Canada had the slowest proportional increase in housing completions of any country in the group. Certainly that is no record to be proud of.

speechtext:
I am glad the minister asked that question because it leads me to my next point. Why is the cost of housing so high in Canada? We find in the report of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, to which I previously referred, that Canadians are forced to spend a greater percentage of the consumer dollar on rent than the peoples of any other industrialized country in North America or western Europe. Why? I think the reasons are not hard to find. They can be found in speculation, in inflated land prices and all the other things that make housing as expensive as it is in Canada. In the past we have not solved the problem. We have created a bonanza for speculators, real estate agents, loan agencies and contractors. But we have not solved the housing problem. The problem grows day by day. It is caused by our rapid growth, by inflated real estate values, by the lack of planning and by the influx of immigrants. The result has been that housing and shelter in this country take more of the consumer dollar than they do in any other country in North America or western Europe.
The proposed amendment making loans available for older houses finally recognizes the need to improve dwellings constantly, to prevent blight from growing in our towns and cities. We have urged this step for a long time. There are many old houses across the country needing only a little maintenance and

improvement, after which they will be as good and every bit as serviceable as any new house that may be built today. There are certain standards, of course, which have to be met. In the past standards have been set for new housing. As I said before, part of the problem is that with these standards and regulations the low income groups are and have been legally barred from taking advantage of the program. There are certain construction standards having to do with the size of buildings and the relationship of one building to another.
If we are to move into the field of older houses standards of maintenance must also be set up. Unfortunately, under the present form of assessment and taxation prevalent in our communities improvement is discouraged and blight is encouraged. People are hesitant about making necessary improvements to their property because the minute they do their assessment skyrockets and up go their taxes. The government must take this into consideration if an effort to cope with this problem is to be made.
The twin factors causing blight are low incomes on the one hand and greedy, uncaring and often unscrupulous landlords on the other. It is interesting to note, and every study will show this, that hardly any of the worst houses in our cities or towns are owner occupied. No matter which part of the country you look at, in the blighted areas you will find that the houses there are tenant occupied rather than owner occupied. Action must be taken in this field if this situation is to be corrected.
The over-all aim of any intelligent program to solve these problems should be by education and voluntary compliance with the regulations. If the government hopes to accomplish anything in this field, it will have to embark on a program of education. Legal enforcement should be the last resort, but it should be clearly understood that there will be legal enforcement where necessary.
Standards vary from place to place and from area to area. What may be suitable in southern Ontario may not be suitable for the northern part of the province. It is very difficult to set down specific standards but I think we should look at the basic essentials. In the report, "A Better Place To Live", sponsored by the Department of Municipal Affairs, Community Planning Branch, and
October 26, 1966

published in June, 1962, it is interesting to note the following on page 13:
The essentials to which Dr. Rose refers were. ..
A.	Fundamental physiological needs: Proper temperature, pure air, adequate natural and artificial light, quiet, adequate space for play and outdoor living.
B.	Fundamental psychological needs:	Adequate
privacy, opportunities for normal family and community life, ease of household operation, maintenance of cleanliness, aesthetic satisfaction.
C.	Protection against contagion: Pure water supply, toilet facilities, interior sanitation, exclusion of vermin, food storage facilities, sufficient sleeping space.
D.	Protection against accidents: Sound construction, fire protection, protection against electrical defects and gas poisonings, injuries in the home, traffic hazards.
These are the basic essentials for any housing program. It is easy to apply these essentials to the construction of new homes. It will not be so easy for older houses under the newly proposed plan, and greater care will have to be taken.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
We must keep in mind that throughout the history of our society we have always been able to create new problems at a greater rate than we have solved old problems. Whether it is atom bombs, automobiles on the highways or space travel, trying to travel to the moon before we learn how to behave among ourselves on earth, that statement holds true. The same thing applies to this field. That is why I urge the government to roll up its sleeves and get cracking. Do not be satisfied with announcing good intentions. Stop kidding yourselves and stop trying to kid the Canadian people. I remind the committee that the Canadian people are not as easy to kid as they used to be.
This is one of the reasons we find such great unrest across the country at the present time. There is unrest in the labour movement because the young people coming into the labour force are not willing to stand for what their fathers stood for all their lives. There is trouble in the political field because the age-old stories which used to go down so well are no longer acceptable. There is growing disillusionment and dissatisfaction with both the old-line political parties.
I urge the government, as I congratulate them on this new move, to follow these good words with good acts and make sure that this bill really works to meet the housing needs of this country.

Mr. Chairman, I shall take a few minutes to put forward my views on this resolution which was long expected by many Canadians.
In introducing his resolution, the minister did not fail to mention the importance of the National Housing Act. I share his views fully, for had it not been for that act, few heads of families even in higher income groups would own their own house today, or else they would have had to pay much more and pay much higher interests to buy it.
However, I regret, as pointed out by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) a while ago, that again the amendment proposed by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) seems to ignore heads of families with low incomes. I intend to deal with that later on in my brief statement. But before doing so, I should like to mention that the government feels the need to raise the percentage of the loans to make it somewhat easier for people to become home owners. In a nutshell, the government is encouraging Canadians to buy their homes.
The minister and the government have doubtless noticed that people avoid purchasing houses. One must wonder why. To my mind, it is not that they do not want to own a home, but rather because they cannot afford it, the cost of building having now become prohibitive compared to their income or salaries.
Mr. Chairman, I feel that the reason for this negligence, if one can call it so-it is not negligence-is that the government does not seem to know what prevents people from buying their homes these days. The cost of houses has gone up chiefly because of the 11 per cent tax on building materials. When the government decided to levy this 11 per cent tax, it knew well enough to offer, at the same time, a $500 bonus on the construction of homes during the winter months.
Recently, the minister and the government cancelled that $500 bonus for winter construction, but they did not remove 11 per cent tax on building materials. The cost of a new home is therefore still considerably higher.
I feel that if the minister had wanted to be logical with himself, had he wanted his amendments to be rational, he would have obtained from the Minister of Finance and Receiver General (Mr. Sharp) and the government removal of that tax. Then, he would have seen that a far greater number of Canadians would have bought new homes.

October 26. 1966
National Housing Act
However, increasing the loan ratio for houses from 85 to 90 per cent of the loan value will certainly allow more workers to buy a new house or one built a few years ago, that is the kind which the minister likes to call "an old house". I congratulate the minister on proposing this amendment through which people who want to buy, improve and occupy a house already built will be able to obtain loans under the same conditions as those who want to buy or build a new house.
Mr. Chairman, this measure has long been awaited; it has long been requested, and I am sure it will be welcomed by the Canadian people for it will allow some of them to buy very soon the house which suits them and which they want and need.
However, we must consider the need for new housing. In 1965, according to statistics, there were 145,570 marriages in Canada, which, to my mind, makes for so many more new dwellings. It was not possible for me to get more recent figures, but I have here the number of private dwellings destroyed by fire in 1962, that is 62,353 dwellings.
Mr. Chairman, if we add to these figures the number of houses-

The point I want to make is the yearly need for new houses. Also, a number of dwellings becoming completely untenantable either due to old age, or because of wind damage, or damage caused by other natural elements which destroy a certain number of dwellings.
However, we must allow for the number of dwellings which are abandoned after the death of the original occupants. These houses are fit for habitation and become available to others.
It is easy to understand that, each year, at least 200,000 new dwellings are needed.

Consequently, I believe this must be our aim, so that every family will be adequately sheltered.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to deal here with that part of the minister's statement where he says that until now loans had been made mostly to people with a high income, above average, and that from now on loans will be granted mostly to people with an annual income of $5,000 or more.
If you look at the figures supplied by the official researchers and if you refer to a certain report published in May 1966, which was prepared by the secretariat for special projects in the war against poverty in Canada, you find this:
According to the definition of "family", given by the census, the income of 23 per cent of Canadian families was less than $3,000 in 1961. Among the families headed by a woman, more than half had an income inferior to $3,000 and about two fifths of them had less than $2,000. Three fishermen families out of five, one lumbermen and farmers family out of two. and one labourer out of three had an income inferior to $3,000.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, that clearly indicates that there is in Canada a very large number of families whose income is inferior to $3,000 per year, who cannot take advantage of the present program announced by the minister and the government to become the owners of a house.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I feel this percentage is high and the government should look into the matter. I admit that the minister pointed out earlier, to the member for Timmins (Mr. Martin), I believe, that those people could live in public or low rental housing. But why could those families not become owners? Why force them to live in poor and unsuitable surroundings? Why must those families always live together in the same environment? Why could they not have the privilege, the right to choose for themselves the surroundings where they are going to live?
I admit that it is another aspect of the problem and the government should see that the income of all Canadians is increased. When we consider the conditions in our villages, towns and cities, we note that this provision of the law enables some landlords, whom I would call sharks, to take advantage of the situation, and make rather considerable profits by renting almost untenantable houses. Those people have to live in slums.

Mr. Chairman, I urge the minister and the government to look into this problem of families with low income, in order to enable them to purchase a house and to become owners, and I think that an aspect of the war against poverty must precisely be that anyone should be in a position to purchase a house or dwelling.
Once again, in the document quoted a moment ago, the author, dealing with housing, says, and rightly so-I noticed it myself very often, and I think that is common knowledge -that houses in general are much too small for the families occupying them.
In the document published in May 1966 and entitled "Aspects of Poverty", we find, on page 4:
In 1961, housing In Canada provided a number of rooms exceeding by one third the number of people, but in 60,000 houses, there were rooms for half the people only.
Mr. Chairman, that document proves that, even for existing housing, there is still much to do in that matter, and this an aspect which needs prompt consideration. I quote again:
Overcrowding, (the number of persons per room), is closely related to the levels of salaries. Only 18 per cent of families with an income of $6,000 or more in 1961, lived in houses providing less than one room per person. Among families whose income was inferior to $3,000 the proportion was 35 per cent.
Mr. Chairman, once again, that proves that for persons having an income under $5,000 a year, it is practically impossible to afford suitable housing, and even when they find housing in community centres, or in the so-called low-rent houses, they must live in houses much too small for their needs.
On page 5 of the same document, we read:
The less suitable houses were mostly occupied by older people-
Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether we give enough consideration to the housing of our pensioners.
In certain important centres, houses are being built for these people and I think that the National Housing Act of 1954, should help promote the building of those houses, but I think that there are still too many restrictions which impede the building of houses of that kind for these people.
I continue, or rather I return to the quotation:
The most inadequate housing units were mainly occupied by old people, divided families and Indians. For instance, 200,000 housing units occupied by people 65 years of age or over had no flush toilets. One divided family out of six had to

share an apartment with others. Only 30 per cent of Indian houses had inside running water and only 9 per cent had inside toilets.
Those figures do not permit a precise assessment to the degree to which people live in completely inadequate houses because they cannot afford anything better in line with their means.
In that respect, there is no doubt that several hundreds of thousands of homes are really needed.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, in view of those facts which have been compiled following some studies on poverty, I think that all possible means should be used to find such facilities and give each head of a family the possibility to house his wife and children in a proper home suited to their needs. Thus can a family progress properly.
The hon. member for Timmins referred a little earlier to a document showing what a home should include. Mr. Chairman, we find today that most of the existing houses fall short of such requirements. Therefore, I think that we should as soon as possible study in depth the housing situation in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks with regard to the resolution which is intended to introduce the amendments to the National Housing Act. I should also like to make a few general comments on the housing situation. May I commend the minister on what he has outlined today in the resolution, if it represents all the amendments which are to be introduced following this discussion. While I believe the changes being introduced definitely are a move in the right direction and certainly provide a far better program than the incentive program, I am most concerned about the over-all picture of housing because I think the whole housing industry in the matter of construction of homes for Canadian people is rapidly falling behind the need. At the beginning I should like to make a few remarks in this regard before commenting on the resolution itself and the statement of the minister.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
According to statistics available, there will be only about 140,000 new units built in Canada in 1966. It is estimated that this will

October 26, 1966
National Housing Act
be 110,000 short of the nation's need. This is a serious situation because it is easier to cut back than it is to begin a building program again.
Another element of the building program which makes the situation more acute is that relating to the fact that houses now being built are of a cost standard far beyond the average wage earners' ability to pay for them. I am not talking only about the wage earner who receives less than $5,000 a year. Even for those making from $5,000 to $10,000 the price of houses is beyond their reach.
I was interested in noting some statistics which came to light just the other day about the constant increase in building costs. In the city of Toronto the average cost of a house sold this year was $27,000. That is up 22 per cent over the last year and a half. Certainly a home of this value is not only beyond the ability to buy of the wage earner who receives less than $5,000 per year; it is available only to those who actually earn $10,000 or more per year. The situation is rapidly developing into a crisis and will soon become one of our major problems in Canada.
It seems to be rather a paradox that, when we have such an abundance of building materials of every type one cares to mention and construction organizations, we are denied a sufficient number of homes because of a tight money policy. There is truly a crisis in the homebuilding industry and it is becoming more and more acute.
The minister said in his remarks today that the financial and economic policy of the government is directed toward warding off the threat of a dangerous inflation. He admitted that it is really the tight money policy which is in many ways restricting the industry and that in some measure he is attempting to solve the problem through these national housing amendments. I think that is a wrong philosophy, but I know that the minister who has presented this resolution is not personally responsible for this policy. Certainly it is governmental policy that is seriously affecting the present and future economy of the country.
In reading the Montreal Gazette this afternoon I noticed a cartoon in the financial section depicting two sons of the road talking to each other under the shade of a tree. One is saying to the other:
I've thought of going back to work.. .but prosperity brings inflation which begets recession which leads to depression which calls for tight money causing unemployment.. .and I'd be right back where I am now.

In addition to the provisions to be found in this resolution there is an urgent necessity for a financial and economic policy which will remove the problem of tight money which is now preventing the construction of homes at a rate to satisfy the increasing need of the people. We are falling behind by
110,000	units this year, which indicates that something is radically wrong. Not only are we going to be short by 110,000 homes but, as the minister has pointed out, people in the low income brackets are going to have to utilize public housing because they are denied the right to build new homes. Something must be done so they will have no difficulty in purchasing their own homes and carrying the associated financial responsibility.
Having said that, let me also state that I think the alternatives proposed by the minister are sound as far as they go. Certainly it is excellent to provide for the purchasing and rebuilding of older homes. This is one way to help the wage earner in the low income bracket. It will also solve a very real problem which I am told by men in the contracting industry now exists in that it is impossible to move into old sections of our cities and build new homes. Whenever that is done the value of the new home is automatically lowered without increasing the value of those homes which are already there. A program that will provide national housing funds for the purchase and repair of older homes I think is a program devised on a sound basis. As I said earlier, I am sure this will result in greater benefits than did the winter incentive program.
While this program may be good there is another problem involved. In order to meet the housing needs of this nation it will be necessary to move farther out than we have at the present time and build new homes in new districts and perhaps even develop satellite towns. I think this is one of the challenging aspects of a solution to the housing problem in urban centres.
I noted with interest the minister's remarks regarding university housing and the projects that are under way this year which will accommodate some 6,000 students. This is a satisfactory program but it ought to be extended on a broader scale. How can we expect to house the students at our universities unless this program is extended? I was surprised by what the minister said in regard to smaller, private institutions of learning not being eligible for this type of loan. Surely if we are going to avoid discrimination and be fair to one and all it is hardly right that just
October 26, 1966

the larger universities should be included in this program, with the smaller universities and private colleges being ineligible. I hope that will not be the case when the actual bill is placed before us.
There is another area of real need in the housing industry which falls legitimately within the responsibility and scope of reference of our national housing authority. Perhaps this is a municipal problem but it is one involved in providing the necessary expansion in home units across the country. I refer to the cost of land and services essential to any new home. Ten years ago the cost of land in relation to the value of a new house was about 10 per cent. Now that the cost of land and essential services in new areas has increased the relationship has gone up to between 25 per cent and 30 per cent. Surely that is completely out of balance and represents a further need for assistance to municipal authorities for the provision of new land and services in urban areas or satellite towns.
We are waiting with great interest for the introduction of the bill and we hope that as a result of what the minister has said the scope of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in respect of universities and municipalities will be extended to provide these necessary services in new areas, in addition to sewage systems and sewgae disposal plants. The plan to extend the authority of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to include the purchase of repairable homes is only the beginning of a wider program which I think is urgently necessary. Not only is the financial policy of the government unduly and harmfully restrictive at this time, but the situation that exists points up the fact that the authority of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation must be further extended in order that it may have the ability to meet the urgent demand for more housing units.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Again, Mr. Chairman, I remind the minister that there has been a great deal of talk about inflation, but I believe that instead of preventing inflation by reason of the policies of this government, all that is being done is building up inflationary pressures which are working to the detriment of not only the economy but the people themselves. We await with interest the introduction of the legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am very glad indeed to see this resolution come forward and to be able to indicate that we support it. This is the first occasion on which I have had 23033-579
National Housing Act
the opportunity to discuss housing in this new parliament; in fact, it is the first occasion I have had the opportunity to discuss the subject since I ceased to be the minister responsible for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the National Housing Act in April, 1963. Prior to that time I had had some nine months experience and responsibility in this field. I look back with the greatest pleasure to that responsibility.
I would say without hesitation that looking at the proposals embodied in the resolution now before us, and anticipating the bill to be based on that resolution, in all particulars the changes appear to be improvements, and in some respects important improvements, upon the present legislation and programs authorized and in progress under that legislation.
The basis upon which government must approach housing legislation and housing programs in this country is readiness to match with government action the constant need for expansion and improvement in this area. It is amazing, when you look back over the history of this field, how constantly the needs of the country expand and how rapidly they change. I recall, thinking back quickly over the history within my personal knowledge, the improvements made in this field by one of my distinguished predecessors as minister responsible for the National Housing Act, a fellow townsman of the present minister, namely, Hon. Howard Green. I recall that by reason of the impetus and direction he gave in this field, housing starts in 1958 reached a record to that date of 164,632. In fact, Mr. Chairman, this record was not surpassed until seven years later, just last year, 1965, when housing starts reached a level of 165,568.

speechtext:
I am relying upon a report prepared for the Montreal District Homebuilders' Association. The minister says there was just a few hundred difference in 1964, so there is no real quarrel. I am merely emphasizing that the improvements made in 1958 stood until 1964-65, when they were surpassed by an increase of just under 1,000 housing starts. Therefore I think it will be agreed that what was done by my predecessor gave a substantial impetus to the housing industry of this country. Yet I recall that so rapid is the need for change in order to meet the changing requirements in this country

October 26, 1966
National Housing Act
that by the time of my stewardship just four years later a great many more changes and improvements were necessary. Therefore we undertook to overhaul the National Housing Act. I should like to point out to the committee the spirit and enterprise in which that overhaul was undertaken.
I discussed the matter with the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. We agreed that there were very important and obvious areas of need. So I said to them, "I want you to assess the problems in both the short and long term and design, on the basis of your answers to those problems, the best possible housing program. Let us first come forward with recommended changes to the National Housing Act which will be the best we can possibly design on both the short and long term view. Be generous in your concept of what the need is and be forwardlooking in the answers you bring forward to those needs as you see them."
This approach was of course received with great enthusiasm by the officials concerned and it was in that spirit that they brought in the answers, which I recall were embodied in a document of considerable bulk, as can readily be imagined. I said, "Let us not worry about the difficulties that will arise. Obviously difficulties will arise and we cannot get everything we want. Let us put forward the best proposals we can frame, and then it will be my job to worry about how to get them through cabinet and that body known as treasury board."
The document was compiled in this spirit and embodied a very forward-looking program. I recall with distinct pleasure and gratification that it received cabinet approval in principle virtually intact. There were some changes and deletions-these are inevitable in a program of this type-but I had obtained approval to practically the whole document when what I can only call an untoward incident took place in February of 1963 resulting in the fall of the government.
The result was that my successor as minister of public works, the immediate predecessor of the minister responsible at the present time, was the beneficiary of this very fine document. I am happy to be able to record that all the changes recommended in that document, and perhaps one or two others, were incorporated in the amendments to the National Housing Act introduced by the present government in 1964.

I mention this piece of history primarily to emphasize the constant need for improving and updating legislation in this field and the constant need for planning for future growth. Those amendments were introduced in 1964, only three years ago. I recall also that in 1965 other amendments were made, though they were not so far reaching. Now in 1966 the minister is again coming forward with quite substantial recommendations for amendments, modifications and improvements. So it is clear, is it not, that this is a field of constant progress, constant change and one in which governments must be ready to match the needs with action?
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
When we think of particular areas in which it is so obvious that the prospects of growth call for action, I believe we must take very serious account of the forecasts in the field of housing especially. I believe, Mr. Speaker, on the basis of the reports that I have read and that I know other members of the committee have read, it is well within the realm of practical or conservative forecasts that there will be a need for an additional 700,000 or
750,000	units by 1970. Indeed, some forecasts and surveys that I have seen give rise to a reasonably-founded assumption that the need between now and 1970 may reach as many as one million units over and above what is presently available by way of housing accommodation in Canada. I think that even taking into account the lower range of that bracket it is a very formidable program, and we must therefore be prepared to plan on that scale. Although I have said that the proposals before us are improvements, I would have a very real reservation whether they form an adequate basis for planning and programming on the scale which I believe should be undertaken in Canada.
There are one or two other specific observations which I would like to make with respect to this program. While the objectives outlined by the minister also represent improvements and are practical and praiseworthy objectives, I think they leave one area still not covered. I refer primarily to smaller communities across Canada where conventional lenders do not operate. I base my criticism upon what the minister said and I will try to reproduce his statement in summary. He pointed out that the intent of these changes is to ensure that the funds allocated to housing are directed to those areas where the greatest social and economic benefits will follow. There can be no quarrel with that
October 26, 1966

statement of general principle, but it is with the omissions that I find fault. He mentioned specifically housing for aged people and for students, slum and city improvement and the provision of housing accommodation for the new resource based communities.
I am quite sure no one would quarrel with any of those projects being desirable objectives, but it is the omissions which I think are significant. Based upon my own impressions when I was the minister responsible, we still have not made adequate provision for the smaller communities which, because of the lack of conventional lending institutions in this field, are almost entirely dependent upon the direct lending activities of C.M.H.C. These communities have, to my knowledge, consistently lagged behind. To refuse them adequate attention now, while concentrating exclusively on the other areas, means a further deterioration in their relative position.

While I do not minimize for a moment the trend toward building up great metropolitan areas in Canada-this is where the majority of our people will live in the future-it would be folly to concentrate our effort solely in that direction; in fact, it would be foolish and undesirable. There are important elements in the continuing activities of our population being carried on in these smaller communities and, while urbanization should not be discouraged and efforts should be made constantly to improve the conditions of urban areas, a proportionate effort should be made to improve the conditions of those who require improved housing in the smaller communities across Canada.

This problem has already been dealt with by the hon. member for Red Deer so I shall not elaborate on it. I agree with him that this area has not been sufficiently covered by these proposals. Finally, I should like to say that one of the other important areas not adequately dealt with in this bill is in the realm of assistance to builders and municipalities in enabling them to provide sites for new housing and new urban development. Greater assistance and flexibility are needed with respect to the standards of servicing and the provision of servicing in those new sites. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOAN RATIO ON RENTAL HOUSING, LOANS ON EXISTING HOUSING, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the resolution stage of the new housing legislation I would like to welcome the new features of policy which are found in the resolution introduced by the minister. I want to mention in particular the provision for loans for student housing projects, which are no longer to be restricted to accommodation for university students, and to the provision for the purchase and improvement of existing housing.
As the minister is well aware, a substantial development of regional technical institutes has taken place in Canada. This is a development which all of us who are interested in the education and training of our young people welcome. But the development brings with it the problem of accommodating the students of these technical institutes.
A good example of this problem is found in metropolitan Toronto where Ryerson Polytechnical Institute now has an enrolment of more than 4,000 day students, about half of whom come from outside metropolitan Toronto and in fact from all parts of Canada. The availability of suitable residential facilities for these students has been deteriorating yearly as the student body has grown. Both federal and provincial governments have been contributing to the expansion of the program at Ryerson. The most recently announced expansion involves an expenditure of about $27 million for new instructional and administrative facilities, but of course the need for accommodating these students is growing at an alarming rate together with the expansion.
Therefore I welcome the minister's proposal that the loans which have been available for students' accommodation at universities be

October 26. 1966
National Housing Act
extended to technical institutes and to other post-secondary institutions which are developing so rapidly in our country and will form such an important part of our educational system.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The proposal to extend loans to persons purchasing and improving existing housing will, I think, be welcomed generally across the country. It has been noted that the upper income groups seem to be well served in their housing needs, that the lower income group is being served better and better by public housing, but that the large middle group representing perhaps 50 per cent of our total population is finding difficulty in obtaining either private or public housing. Lower cost private housing is normally provided by existing aging housing stock, and the proposal of the minister will make this stock more readily available to the large middle group of our population.
I suggest to the minister that the limitation on the loans which has been suggested might be reconsidered. It does seem to me that a top limit of $10,000 might perhaps be inadequate in many of the urban areas of Canada where the cost of even aging houses is substantially higher than that. I hope the minister will consider making some provision for more flexibility in the amount which can be made available under this program.
I believe that housing is a matter of vital national concern, although perhaps primarily a provincial responsibility. I am glad that the government, through its action in the past three years, has demonstrated its recognition of housing and urban development as matters of national importance. I hope that the development of federal interest and involvement in this field will mature before long into a full-fledged department of housing and urban affairs. I believe this would focus national attention and energy, as they need to be focused, on this very vital factor in our national life and growth.
I need hardly point out to hon. members that Canada is rapidly becoming an urban country. We are told that today seven out of ten Canadians live in urban areas, that by 1980 perhaps 70 per cent or 80 per cent of our population will live in urban centres of 30,000 or more. By the turn of the century about half of all Canadians will probably live in only nine huge cities. A prominent consultant and planner, Mr. Murray Jones, has described our society as being on the urban frontier. He

said we are still in the early stages of the devastating fact that by the next generation there will be no heritage other than the urban heritage. In addition, he states that for the first time in history practically everyone will be born and grow up in an urban environment, and that the sheer numbers involved are already bringing increasing evidence of social ills from the tensions and conflicts of large urban areas.
I believe that urban development is so basic to the quality of life in our country that it must be a matter of great national concern. I urge the minister and the government to continue the increased interest and concentration on the problems of urban areas which have been shown over the past few years. I urge the government to treat the problems of urban areas and the problems of housing as matters of the highest priority for the national government. I believe that in doing so it must recognize that the cities are in fact the new frontier of our country.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOAN RATIO ON RENTAL HOUSING, LOANS ON EXISTING HOUSING, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we in the New Democratic Party welcome the amendments to the National Housing Act which are proposed in the resolution put forward by the minister. The minister stated that the National Housing Act had played a most impressive role. However, he underlined the necessity of making a greater impact in the future. We in this party certainly agree with those statements, especially that future amendments are necessary. One of the weaknesses of the National Housing Act has been the philosophy of the government with regard to its role. It still feels that it plays the role of the friendly banker. We disagree with this philosophy and think the government should take leadership in connection with the problems of housing by setting forth a national housing policy to take care of the housing needs of all Canadians.
It would be trite to say that there is a housing shortage in Canada. The figures presented by the minister this afternoon indicate how urgently housing is required. It is very disappointing to know that at the end of nine months there has been a 23 per cent decrease in housing from the figures for 1965. I well remember the statement of the minister in which he said that he contemplated a 10 per cent decrease in housing for the year 1966.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOAN RATIO ON RENTAL HOUSING, LOANS ON EXISTING HOUSING, ETC.
