Did I not say 10 per cent to 15 per cent?
October 26, 1966

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOAN RATIO ON RENTAL HOUSING, LOANS ON EXISTING HOUSING, ETC.
speechtext:
All right, I will accept that, Mr. Chairman. He said from 10 per cent to 15 per cent, but at the moment we are experiencing a 23 per cent decrease which is not very encouraging. I think I should also put on the record the attitude of the minister with regard to the Canadian housing blight as revealed in an article in Canadian Labour for March, 1966. According to the article the minister stated in Toronto in December, 1964:
For all the talk about what we intend to do, for all our efforts, nearly 100,000 Canadian families live every waking moment of their lives under housing conditions that are really appalling-a disgrace to the communities in which they reside. The same 100,000 families cannot find other accommodation on the open market at rents they can afford to pay, and 20 per cent of all our occupied dwellings have very primitive bathing and toilet facilities. This, I suggest, is real poverty.
And quite apart from the despair and degradation of blight and decay, these neglected areas impose an unnecessary drain on the civic economy. Municipal services and other facilities cost more to provide, while assessments must decline. The extra overhead is subsidized by the taxpayers of the entire municipality-assessments must be increased in good areas to offset diminishing tax revenues in the run-down areas.
This is the attitude of the present minister with regard to housing problems, and with this we agree. I should like to review briefly some of the proposed amendments outlined in the resolution. We have, first, the suggestion to increase the ratio from 85 per cent to 90 per cent on rental housing. The question arises, where does this extra money come from? It is evident that it will come from the increase from $8.5 billion to $9.5 billion for insured loans. In his statement this afternoon the minister said that most of these moneys will be directed to the building of senior citizens homes, urban redevelopment and the provision of university accommodation.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
With regard to urban redevelopment, which includes public housing, the main problem is to get sufficient money to sponsor projects. If the money is to come from these insured loans and there is a prevailing rate under the National Housing Act of 6| per cent, it is very difficult to persuade conventional lenders who are lending money at 8 per cent to participate in urban redevelopment programs.
One of the major faults of urban redevelopment has been that the federal government has placed complete responsibility for urban redevelopment upon the municipality without setting forth any guidelines. According to section 23 (I) of the National
National Housing Act
Housing Act, the municipalities are given the power to acquire and to clear lands for urban renewal. The definition of urban renewal is "a blighted or substandard area of a municipality". Yet no guide lines as to what is meant by "blighted or substandard area" are given. In other words, no provision is made for rehabilitation of homes save and except by means of home improvement loans, which are at a maximum of $4,000.
The minister said that most of his suggestions came from symposia. I recommend to him that the government change the definition of "urban renewal scheme". I suggest that he use the definition in section 20 (1) (b) of the planning act of Ontario, which states:
-"redevelopment area" means an area within a municipality, the redevelopment of which in the opinion of the Council is desirable because of age, dilapidation, overcrowding, faulty arrangement, unsuitability of buildings or for any other reason.
This would give the municipality much more scope in dealing with blighted areas under the act.
One of the striking features of urban redevelopment has taken place in Toronto in my riding. The main problem which confronted the Napier Place development was that of relocation. Here was an urban renewal scheme which had no plans for the relocation of the people of the area, who were mainly senior citizens. No accommodation was provided to which they could go while the public housing was constructed, and this imposed serious hardship on them. Second, many of the older folk were content to remain in the area but as a result of the expropriation proceedings were required to buy other homes. This imposed great hardship upon them because of the increased cost and the necessity of assuming a new mortgage. I should like to see the minister take some initiative in this problem by providing interest free loans to persons who are required to move as a result of urban redevelopment to cover the difference between what they receive upon expropriation and what they are required to pay for a new home.
I am sure the minister has heard many representations with regard to the problem of compensation as a result of urban redevelopment. Compensation has been interpreted by a provincial statute as the value to the owner, which is very difficult to define. I would ask the minister to give serious consideration to including in any urban redevelopment scheme provisions to deal with the 10 per cent who are forced to take compensation by reason of expropriation of property.

October 26, 1966
National Housing Act
Another major problem with urban redevelopment which the minister should take into account is the lack of money for recreational and social welfare facilities, as well as for the construction of schools. The main burden of providing recreational facilities and schools in redeveloped areas should not fall upon the municipality. I think the government should participate in the provision of money to build recreational and social facilities and new schools.
With regard to the amendment concerning older homes, the three conditions relating to the provision of financing are (1) purchase, (2) possession and (3) improvement. In his statement this afternoon the minister said this provision should help people with income over $5,000. I remind the minister that the average income last year of a borrower under the National Housing Act was $6,665; he was aged 35 years, married, with two children. In view of his statement in Vancouver that the maximum loan would be $10,000 and that of that amount $2,000 would have to be applied to improvements, I respectfully submit to him that it would be very difficult to apply this formula to places like Toronto. According to his own statement homes range in value between $17,000 and $25,000, and this is certainly the case in Toronto.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, when the minister brings forward this legislation I hope he does not restrict the maximum loan to $10,000 or apply the Same standards which are imposed in respect of new homes. Otherwise he will find that very little advantage is being obtained by the purchase of older homes vis-a-vis the occupation and improvement of them.
It would be unfair to say that home improvement loans have served their purpose adequately. In the report of C.M.H.C. last year it was indicated that for the fourth year there had been a serious decline in the number of loans granted under the act. The maximum loan is $4,000. If people are to improve homes it is essential that additional money be provided for the purchase. Many people who buy older property take out at least one mortgage, and many have two or three. Therefore the government must take active steps to take care of this very important problem.
In connection with increasing the amount of government-insured loans from $8.5 billion

to $9.5 billion, an increase of $1 billion, if we are to depend on insured loans, as the minister says, from the traditional or conventional companies we will have to impose upon them the altruistic spirit of shifting from their present interest rate of 74 to 8 per cent back to 6f per cent. The minister mentioned in his statement that one of the reasons we are having a real housing problem is the competitive interest rates prevailing. I hope that the minister can persuade the insurance companies to shift from an interest rate of 74 to 8 per cent to 6J per cent so that Canadians may be supplied with their housing needs. At the moment I have very little faith in that shifting taking place.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
The next point is with regard to the increase of direct loans under C.M.H.C. I notice the figure is $750 million. If the average loan is to be $15,000 that means that there can be only 50,000 loans for homes. In Toronto alone the need is for 40,000 homes a year.
I quote from page 15 of the Monetary Times of October, 1966:
Toronto, which absorbs 125 new arrivals a day, needs 40,000 new homes a year. So critical is the demand, real estate salesmen have taken to pounding doors almost begging owners to sell. Homes in some areas have appreciated 20% just this year. Rents are soaring, and so too are prices. By normal budgeting yardsticks no Torontonian earning less than $10,000 can "comfortably" buy a new home.
If this is so, with Toronto needing 40,000 homes and the increase permitting roughly 50,000, it does not appear that the housing needs of Canadians will be adequately taken care of. It is interesting to note, speaking of Toronto, that the article refers to people earning $10,000. I ask the minister to tell the house how this legislation will take care of those people in the $5,000 to $10,000 bracket. When the minister suggests that public housing takes care of people earning less than $5,000, he is not basing his argument on facts.
We welcome the change increasing the amount for student housing projects from $200 million to $350 million. A severe restriction has been applied to university housing and the change to take care of students' housing is welcome, as is the change with respect to housing for other than university students.
I believe that the minister has received much correspondence with regard to Ryerson Polytechnical Institute in Toronto. I should like to quote from a letter received by most
October 26, 1966

hon. members, written by D. S. Simmons, chairman of the board of governors. He says in the second paragraph:
Our present enrolment is 4,200 day students. Half of these students come from outside Metropolitan Toronto. The availability of suitable private residential facilities for the students is not good and is deteriorating yearly. As you are perhaps aware, the board has recently announced an expansion program involving an expenditure of approximately $27 million for new instructional and administrative facilities. We are projecting for an increase in enrolment to the 10,000 level within the next five years.
That is almost three times the number of students they have today. I continue quoting:
Our need is, of course, pressing but is obviously growing at an alarming rate. Both the federal and provincial governments are contributing to this expansion program but our first concern is to provide instructional space. None of the $27 million I refer to will be devoted to residences. The board feels it must now pursue actively the matter of residential facilities.
We could not agree more fully, and we are encouraged by the leadership shown by the government in this legislation. We ask that increases continue to be made available to meet this pressing problem.
The final point I wish to make is with regard to the extension of the three-year forgiveness period to municipalities with respect to sewage projects. The report of the minister with regard to the number of municipalities taking advantage of this program is most encouraging. Certainly the government must be given full credit for extending the period.
What I have been saying in the last 15 minutes is that there is an urgent requirement for a federal ministry of urban affairs and housing. It is encouraging to note that during the last election the hon. member for St. Paul's said the same thing. During one of our debates the hon. member for Hamilton West mentioned this and today the hon. member for York-Scarborough repeated it. I am the fourth person to ask for a federal department of urban affairs and housing. Also, we should like to see C.M.H.C. directly responsible to a minister who can set forth a national housing policy, co-ordinate the housing needs of the provinces and municipalities, and set up a program to meet the social and economic needs of all Canadians in the housing field today. We look forward with bated breath to the amendments that will be set forth in the bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was glad to hear the minister mention the importance of adequate housing in the resource growth areas of this country. He made reference to one such community currently under development in my own constituency-one of the instant towns, to use a phrase which has become current in British Columbia. I hope his words will be borne out by the effect of this legislation, especially as to the provision of adequate funds. Many of those who have entered areas where mineral and forest resources have been newly developed have encountered difficulty in securing adequate housing. For many years the concept was held in British Columbia and, indeed, across most of Canada, that men entering resource producing areas could be expected to leave their families and homes behind them for a long period, and be content with inadequate types of bunkhouse accommodation. Though there has been a change in outlook in this respect, the fact remains that in many areas of Canada men are being asked to go out and work in circumstances where normal home and community life are completely absent.
It will be a long time before those who are responsible for the production of so much of the basic wealth of this country can expect to enjoy the amenities which a great many of our citizens take for granted in our urban centres. Large scale projects of housing development have been assisted by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation with the result that real planning has been made possible in communities such as the one at Gold River which the minister mentioned specifically. There are others in my constituency. However, there are communities which have been in existence over a long period where

these large scale undertakings have not developed to the same extent despite the fact that they have lately been growing in size and importance as a result of increased activity in the logging and mining fields.
I suggest that the program for the provision of housing in resource communities has been less adequate in these communities of longer standing than in certain other areas where completely planned communities have been built from scratch. I hope that as a result of this legislation steps will be taken to improve the situation in the older communities, making it easier for individuals and small builders to acquire adequate funds with which to provide necessary housing.
In this connection I remind the minister of a discussion he and I had a few months ago about the problems faced by a school board on Vancouver Island with respect to the provision of housing for the teachers it was hoped to attract to teach in a newly organized senior secondary school. I can inform the minister that the particular problem I discussed with him has been overcome and that the school is now in operation, with some fine teachers on the staff. Nevertheless, I point out that this was not done as a result of any aid by public housing authorities of Canada. Indeed, it was in spite of rather than because of those authorities that this was achieved. I hope that one of the results of this resolution will be to make housing money more easily available in adequate quantities in circumstances of this kind.
I receive a good many complaints about the high cost of the financial arrangements entered into for the provision of housing. Some of the housing which is being built is good according to ordinary Canadian standards but the high cost to those who need homes either for purchase or for rent is still a grave barrier.
The resolution mentions the improvement of older homes so that those whose incomes are neither above nor below certain levels may be assisted. In the new resource communities there are no older homes to be purchased, remodelled or improved. The increase may therefore not be sufficient to enable applicants to acquire new houses under the arrangements which have prevailed in the past. This is a serious problem and it has to be considered in connection with the continuous increase which has taken place in the level of interest rates, against which members of this party have spoken many times.
